items.question: A teammate adds role="button" and an onclick handler to a div and calls it done. Is it?
items.answer: No. The role only changes how the element is mapped in the accessibility tree; it adds no behavior. The div is still not focusable, does not activate on Enter or Space, and lacks every other native button behavior, so tabindex, key handlers, and state must be hand-built. That is exactly the JavaScript and ARIA a native button gives you for free, which is why the default is the correct HTML element.
items.trap: The naive belief is that an ARIA role brings the element's behavior with it. It changes the announcement, not the interaction: keyboard and assistive-technology users get a control they can hear but cannot operate. MDN states it directly: adding ARIA semantics only exposes information to the accessibility API and does not affect the page's DOM (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA).

items.question: A design shows a whole card as clickable, with a title, an image, and a secondary link inside. How do you build it without wrecking semantics?
items.answer: Keep the card a non-interactive container and make its primary action a real link or button whose hit area covers the card via CSS, while the secondary action stays a separate real control. CSS can stretch the primary control's presentation without changing the meaning of the markup. Building a custom control is the last resort, for when native HTML cannot express the interaction.
items.trap: The common shortcuts both fail: wrapping the entire card in an anchor nests interactive elements inside interactive elements, and putting role="button" on the card div recreates button behavior by hand. Both trade a free native control for custom behavior that must be implemented, tested, and maintained.

items.question: A page has a header navigation, a breadcrumb, and a footer navigation, all as nav elements. Screen-reader users hear 'navigation' three times. What do you do?
items.answer: Give repeated regions of the same type distinguishing labels, for example aria-label="Primary", "Breadcrumb", and "Footer" on each nav, so the landmark list shows three distinguishable entries and users can jump directly to the one they want.
items.trap: Hoping the landmark list or the links inside each nav will disambiguate: unlabeled same-type landmarks are announced identically, so users must explore each one to find the navigation they need. The label is what makes repeated landmarks usable.

items.question: A screen-reader user reports your page 'jumps from heading level 1 to level 4'. The visual design uses three font sizes that do not map to h2, h3, h4. What went wrong and what do you change?
items.answer: Heading levels were chosen to match the mockup's font sizes instead of the document outline. Fix the markup so levels reflect the actual content hierarchy, and restyle the sizes in CSS. Also re-check the source order, because screen-reader reading order follows the document, not the visual arrangement.
items.trap: Picking levels by font size feels harmless because the page looks right, but users navigating by headings get an outline that misrepresents the page, with apparently missing sections. Font size is a CSS concern; heading level is structure.

items.question: An input has a visible label reading 'Email address' and also aria-label="Contact email". Which name do screen readers announce, and why can that be a problem?
items.answer: They announce 'Contact email'. In the accessible name computation, aria-label takes precedence over an associated label element, so the visible label is replaced, not combined. Keep them consistent: WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name expects the visible label text to be part of the accessible name, because speech-input users say what they see (https://www.w3.org/TR/accname-1.2/, https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/label-in-name.html).
items.trap: Most people assume the visible label always wins, or that both are announced. Neither happens: the override is silent, so a sighted screen-reader user hears one thing and sees another, and a voice-control user who says 'click Email address' may get no match.

items.question: The design marks required fields with a red asterisk only. How do you make 'required' perceivable without guessing?
items.answer: Expose it programmatically with the native required attribute (or aria-required for custom controls) so the state is announced, keep any visible convention like the asterisk explained in text near the top of the form or in the label, and never rely on color alone. Group related controls with fieldset and legend so radio and checkbox sets also announce their group context.
items.trap: The asterisk is a visual convention with no programmatic tie to the control, so it is never announced and its meaning is only available to sighted users who happened to read the explanation. Color plus an unexplained symbol fails both machine checks and human checks.

items.question: The team wants to disable the submit button until every client-side constraint passes, to prevent invalid submissions. Why is that an accessibility problem?
items.answer: Disabled controls are not focusable and their state is not necessarily perceived or explained, so keyboard and screen-reader users can reach a silent dead end with no idea what is wrong. Keep the button enabled, validate on submission, and return specific, visible errors associated with each affected control. The server must validate everything anyway, because client-side constraints are a usability feature, not a security boundary.
items.trap: 'It prevents invalid submissions' is the reasoning teams use, but disabling hides the reason for failure and removes the control from the tab order, so the user gets nothing to act on. The server still needs the identical validation regardless.

items.question: Server validation fails and you render the errors client-side. How do you connect each message to its field?
items.answer: Keep the label as the field's name and attach the message text with aria-describedby so it is announced when the user focuses the field. Make errors visible, specific, and not communicated by color alone, and after a failed submission make an error summary or the first invalid field reachable without an unexpected focus jump, preserving the entered values.
items.trap: Rendering a red border plus a message in a distant div feels sufficient because it looks like an error UI, but neither piece is programmatically associated with the control, so focusing the field announces nothing, and color carries the error alone.

items.question: flex-wrap: wrap gives me rows and columns. Isn't that two-dimensional layout, same as Grid?
items.answer: No. Wrapped flex lines are independent: items in one line do not align with items in the next, and there is no column axis to size or place against. Grid models rows and columns together, so when alignment across both axes matters, Grid expresses the relationship and Flexbox does not.
items.trap: Confusing visual wrapping with a two-dimensional model. The layout looks grid-like in a screenshot, but as soon as content lengths differ, the wrapped rows drift out of alignment because there are no shared column tracks.

items.question: A flex child with flex: 1 overflows its parent when it contains a long unbreakable string. Why?
items.answer: flex: 1 sets flex-basis to 0, but flex items default to min-width: auto, so the item cannot shrink below its min-content width and long content forces overflow. Fix the item with min-width: 0 (plus overflow-wrap or an overflow strategy), not the parent. This is exactly the class of bug you only catch by testing long content and narrow widths rather than trusting a screenshot (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/min-width).
items.trap: The instinct is to blame flex-basis or the container and add hacks there. The culprit is the implicit min-content floor on the flex item itself, so container-level fixes leave the overflow in place.

items.question: After using order to show the sidebar first, tabbing feels wrong. Can positive tabindex values fix the focus order?
items.answer: No. Fix the HTML source order and use CSS to create the presentation. Positive tabindex creates a separate order that jumps ahead of every zero-index control, is hard to maintain, and does not change screen-reader reading order, so the mismatch survives the patch.
items.trap: Reaching for tabindex feels like a surgical fix, but it layers a second ordering system on top of the mismatch instead of removing the mismatch, and it breaks again as soon as the layout or the markup changes.

items.question: Is order the only property with this source-order risk?
items.answer: No. Grid placement (grid-template-areas, line placement), flex-direction row-reverse and column-reverse, and any other visual reordering mechanism decouple visual order from DOM order the same way. Treat order and grid placement as visual tools only; if the logical order is wrong, the fix belongs in the HTML.
items.trap: Teams audit for order, find none, and ship row-reverse or grid areas that reorder content. The user-facing failure, focus that appears to jump and a reading order that differs from the visual one, is identical.

items.question: To stop iOS zooming into inputs, a teammate adds maximum-scale=1 and user-scalable=no to the viewport meta. What is wrong, and what is the actual fix?
items.answer: Blocking zoom removes a primary low-vision strategy and conflicts with the ability to resize text. The auto-zoom is triggered by focusing inputs whose font size is below the browser's threshold, 16px in iOS Safari, so the fix is font-size: 16px on inputs, textareas, and selects. Keep zoom available and test the page zoomed (https://css-tricks.com/16px-or-larger-text-prevents-ios-form-zoom).
items.trap: 'It stops the annoying zoom' treats the symptom as the problem. Pinch-zoom is an accessibility requirement for many users, and the input zoom the team was actually fighting has a font-size fix that removes no capability.

items.question: Where does unexpected horizontal scrolling usually come from in a supposedly responsive page, and how do you find it?
items.answer: Fixed widths, oversized media, and flex or grid items that cannot shrink below their min-content size (the same min-width: auto floor). Find it by testing intermediate widths, zoom, and long localized strings rather than a few device screenshots, and fix it with relative units, min-width: 0 where items must shrink, and sensible minimum and maximum sizes.
items.trap: Screenshot passes at a handful of popular widths miss it, because overflow appears at odd in-between widths and with long content. 'Looks fine at 390px and 1440px' is not the same as 'never scrolls horizontally'.

items.question: Which wins: :where(#promo, .card) a { color: navy } or .card a { color: teal }?
items.answer: Teal. :where() contributes zero specificity, so the ID and class inside it are discarded for the comparison and the whole rule counts as just the type selector a, which is (0,0,1). .card a is (0,1,1) and wins. The arguments inside :where() only widen what matches; they add no weight.
items.trap: Counting the ID inside :where() is the reflex, because an ID normally dominates. Inside :where() the argument list is match-only, so even an ID there loses to a single class elsewhere.

items.question: Your reset lives in @layer reset, but a later unlayered rule overrides it even though the layered selector is more specific. Why does the layer lose?
items.answer: For normal declarations from the same origin, the cascade compares cascade layers before specificity, and unlayered author styles rank above all layered author styles, so the unlayered rule wins regardless of selector weight. Express the precedence you want as layer order, or move overrides into a later layer, instead of escalating specificity. Note that !important flips this relationship for important declarations (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer).
items.trap: The reflex is to add IDs or !important inside the layer to 'win on specificity'. The layer comparison happens first, so escalation inside the losing layer cannot rescue a normal declaration; it just poisons the stylesheet for future overrides.

items.question: Does CSS nesting change specificity? Is .card { & a { color: teal } } stronger than .card a?
items.answer: No. Nesting is syntactic sugar: the browser generates the equivalent descendant selector .card a, with identical specificity. What nesting does change is how easily you write long, high-specificity chains without noticing, which is why you still inspect the generated selector specificity rather than trusting the indentation (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_nesting/Using_CSS_nesting).
items.trap: Coming from CSS-in-JS or preprocessors, people assume nesting adds weight or creates scoping. It creates neither, so a 'nested override' can silently lose to a flat selector written elsewhere.

items.question: :has() would let a form group style its title red when it contains an invalid input. How do you ship that safely?
items.answer: As progressive enhancement behind @supports selector(:has(*)): the enhanced rule applies only where supported, and the base experience must already be acceptable without it. Pair it with a documented browser-support policy and tests for focus, zoom, contrast, overflow, and reduced-motion preferences, because a newer feature is not automatically a better abstraction.
items.trap: Shipping the selector unguarded works until an unsupported browser drops the entire rule, because an unsupported selector invalidates the whole rule. If the red title was load-bearing rather than enhancement, the failure state silently loses meaning instead of degrading gracefully.

items.question: An automated audit reports zero violations. Is the page conformant?
items.answer: No conclusion follows. Automated checks cover a repeatable subset of rules; keyboard operation, focus and reading order, alt-text quality, name and state correctness, and real assistive-technology behavior all require manual judgment. Use automation for regression coverage and pair it with manual keyboard and screen-reader passes.
items.trap: A clean scan feels like a certificate, but most criteria ask questions a rule engine cannot answer, such as whether the alt text conveys the right meaning or whether the focus order makes sense. Passing the tool says nothing about those.

items.question: aria-hidden="true" is added to a container that includes a button that is still focusable. What do keyboard screen-reader users experience?
items.answer: The button stays in the tab order, because aria-hidden does not remove focusability, but it is exposed with no name or role, so users tab into a silent, invisible stop. Hiding a focusable element this way is an explicit ARIA usage violation. Either keep the button outside the hidden subtree or hide it with the hidden attribute or display: none, which removes it from the tab order as well (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-hidden).
items.trap: The assumption is that 'hidden from assistive technology' means 'gone'. It only removes the accessibility-tree entry, leaving a keyboard-reachable control that announces nothing, which is worse than either alternative.

items.question: Does adding aria-label="filters" to a plain non-interactive div give screen-reader users anything?
items.answer: Generally no. A generic div has no role that participates in naming, and aria-label is in practice only supported on interactive elements, widgets, landmarks, images, and iframes, so most screen readers ignore it there. Put the label on something that can be named: a real heading, a landmark, or the interactive control itself (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-label).
items.trap: Treating aria-label as a caption you can stick anywhere. Without a role that supports naming, the attribute never reaches users, so the team believes the region is labeled while nothing is announced.

items.question: A button shows the visible text 'Submit' and carries aria-label="Send". What is announced, and why is that a problem?
items.answer: 'Send'. The name computation prefers aria-label over the element's content, so the visible text is replaced. Speech-input users who say 'click Submit' may get no match, because WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name expects the visible label text to be contained in the accessible name. Make them identical, or start the accessible name with the visible text (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/label-in-name.html).
items.trap: The reflex is that visible text always wins, or that both are read out. Neither happens: the override is silent, so the mismatch is invisible to sighted developers and only surfaces with real screen-reader and voice-control testing.

items.question: You need to attach a longer hint ('We will only use this for order updates') to an input. aria-labelledby or aria-describedby?
items.answer: aria-describedby. It adds a description announced after the field, while the label stays the concise accessible name. aria-labelledby would replace the name with the whole sentence, so every navigation of the field reads a paragraph instead of its identity. The same describedby pattern is where error messages belong (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-describedby).
items.trap: Reaching for labelledby because it 'also connects text to the field' misses that it changes what the field is called. Name and description are different slots in the accessibility contract, and swapping them degrades every later interaction.

items.question: A designer asks you to remove the focus outline because it looks bad. When is outline: none acceptable?
items.answer: Only when it is replaced immediately with an equally visible, contrasting focus treatment, for example a custom outline or shadow on :focus-visible. Every keyboard-focusable control needs a visible indicator for as long as focus is present, so removal without replacement is never acceptable.
items.trap: The usual justification is 'we have hover styles'. Hover does nothing for keyboard users; without a replacement indicator, keyboard users lose the only signal telling them where they are on the page.

items.question: Does adding tabindex="0" to a div make it accessible?
items.answer: No. It becomes focusable but still has no role and no name, so screen readers announce nothing meaningful at that stop, and activation still has to be hand-built. A custom control needs an interactive role, a programmatically determinable name, keyboard activation, a sensible place in the tab order, and a visible focus indicator, all together. If a native button, link, or input fits, that is the safer choice.
items.trap: Equating focusability with accessibility. A tab stop that announces nothing is worse than no stop at all: users tab into a silent void and conclude the page is broken.

items.question: What is the practical difference between alt="", a missing alt attribute, and role="presentation" on an img?
items.answer: alt="" is an intentional declaration that the image is decorative, so assistive technology skips it. A missing alt is unspecified: screen readers may announce the filename or the image's presence, forcing users to guess. role="presentation" or role="none" also strips the image's semantics, but the empty alt is the first-line, broadly supported way to say 'decorative'.
items.trap: Omitting alt 'to keep it quiet' achieves the opposite: omission is ambiguity, not decoration, and the filename may get read aloud instead of silence.

items.question: A logo image sits inside the home link, and the word 'Home' is visible next to it. What should the img's alt be?
items.answer: Empty. The link already gets its accessible name from the visible 'Home' text, and alt text inside a link contributes to the link's name, so 'Home' or 'ACME logo' would make the link announce twice or replace better text. If the logo were the link's only content, its alt should give the destination ('Home'), not describe the pixels ('Company logo').
items.trap: Describing the image 'because alt text should describe the image'. Inside a link, alt is the link's name, so description for description's sake degrades navigation instead of helping it.

items.question: After a user action, a status div is created and filled with text in the same operation, but nothing is announced. Why might that happen?
items.answer: Live-region announcements are most reliable when the region already exists in the accessibility tree before its content changes. A region inserted and populated at the same time is not reliably picked up across browser and screen-reader combinations. Keep a persistent region, for example one with role="status", in the DOM and update its text, then verify with the exact browser and screen-reader pair you ship to (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Guides/Live_regions).
items.trap: Assuming aria-live is a queue you can attach at announcement time. The mutation must happen inside a region the accessibility layer was already watching, so 'create then fill' silently fails in common setups.

items.question: When is aria-live="assertive" actually justified?
items.answer: Rarely: only for urgent, time-sensitive messages where interrupting the user is the right call, for example a session about to expire or a destructive action about to run. Routine feedback such as 'Saved' or 'Results updated' should be polite, so it waits for the current utterance instead of trampling it.
items.trap: Using assertive 'to make sure messages are not missed' confuses hearing with understanding. Interruption cuts off whatever the user was reading, and routine assertive updates make the interface unusable with a screen reader.

items.question: A tooltip appears on hover of an info icon and disappears before the pointer can reach it. Which requirement is missed, and what are the others?
items.answer: Hoverable: the pointer must be able to move into the revealed content without it disappearing. The full set for content shown on hover or focus is dismissible (Esc or moving away dismisses it without advancing focus or the pointer), hoverable, and persistent (it stays until dismissed, the trigger is left, or it is no longer valid). All three must hold for keyboard, touch, zoom, and assistive technology, not only a mouse (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/).
items.trap: Teams remember the keyboard half, dismissible, and ship a tooltip that still cannot be reached with a pointer. The user sees the content appear and vanish with no way to read or select it.

items.question: Why style :focus-visible instead of :focus for the custom focus indicator?
items.answer: :focus applies on every focus, including mouse clicks, so a custom ring shows in places where it adds noise and designers then demand its removal. :focus-visible matches when the browser determines an indicator is appropriate, typically keyboard interaction, keeping click interactions clean while keyboard users still always get a visible indicator.
items.trap: Styling :focus everywhere and later deleting the indicator 'because it shows on click too'. The right fix is the more precise pseudo-class plus a sufficiently clear replacement style, never outline: none with nothing behind it.

items.question: We replaced the divs with semantic elements and rankings did not move. Was the refactor pointless?
items.answer: No, but the expectation was wrong. Semantic markup is a foundation: it gives browsers, assistive technology, and other tools clearer content signals and usually improves usability and accessibility, which is why SEO basics and accessibility often align. It is not a promise of a ranking position, which depends on many factors outside your markup.
items.trap: Treating semantics as an SEO trick that should pay out directly. Its value is honest, machine-readable structure; measuring it only by ranking movement misjudges what it does.

items.question: The marketing navigation is built from clickable spans wired up by JavaScript. Why does that hurt crawlers and screen-reader users alike?
items.answer: Real links with hrefs carry the semantics: a destination, keyboard and assistive-technology activation, and a crawlable URL. Span-based navigation only works after JavaScript runs, so the destinations are invisible to tools that do not execute it, and the keyboard and screen-reader affordances of a link are gone.
items.trap: 'It works in the browser' is taken as 'it works'. Anything that does not run the script, including assistive technology and many crawlers, sees a page whose primary navigation does not exist.

items.question: The user closes the mobile menu with Escape or its close button. Where should focus go?
items.answer: Back to the menu toggle, when the user initiated the close from inside the panel. Otherwise the focused element inside the now-hidden panel is removed, focus resets to the document start, and keyboard users must re-traverse the page to get back where they were. If focus is already outside the panel, leave it alone.
items.trap: Letting focus fall back to the body feels like a browser detail, but it silently resets the user's place. Returning focus to the toggle is what makes the open and close loop predictable.

items.question: The collapsed panel is hidden by positioning it off-screen with left: -9999px instead of being truly hidden. What is the problem?
items.answer: Off-screen content stays in the accessibility tree and the tab order, so users tab through invisible links and hear a menu that is supposedly closed. Use the hidden attribute or display: none so the closed panel is actually removed from rendering, the tab order, and the accessibility tree.
items.trap: Equating 'invisible' with 'hidden'. Visually off-screen is still fully present for keyboard and assistive-technology users, so the menu is closed for sighted users only.

items.question: Why are viewport media queries the wrong default for a shared card component?
items.answer: The same component renders in a narrow sidebar, a modal, and a full-width region at the same viewport width; its usable space is the container, not the window. Container queries let each instance respond to the space it actually has, so the component adapts to where it lives instead of to a device catalog encoded in breakpoints.
items.trap: Encoding the page's breakpoints into every component. The team guesses viewport widths where each instance probably fits, and the component breaks in any layout the guesses did not cover, which is the device-catalog problem again at component scale.

items.question: A container query switches the card to a horizontal layout at 40rem. What accessibility check does that switch trigger?
items.answer: Verify that the visual reorder does not decouple reading and focus order from DOM order, and re-test keyboard traversal and screen-reader reading at both layouts. Responsive changes must not change the logical focus order; if the horizontal layout reorders content relative to source, the fix is the same as for order and grid placement: correct the source order.
items.trap: Treating the container switch as purely visual because 'it is just CSS'. Any mechanism that reorders content visually creates the same mismatch between what sighted users see and what keyboard and screen-reader users traverse.

items.question: You move focus to the new view's h1 after a client-side route change. Why tabindex="-1" on the heading instead of 0?
items.answer: -1 makes the heading programmatically focusable without adding it to the sequential tab order, which is exactly what a momentary focus destination needs. With 0, the heading becomes a permanent tab stop on every page, adding a keystroke for keyboard users just to support one focus move.
items.trap: Using 0 'to be safe' taxes every keyboard user on every page. The negative value exists precisely for programmatic focus targets that should not be tab stops.

items.question: Why not just fire an aria-live announcement like 'Settings page loaded' on every navigation?
items.answer: Route changes already have a richer established signal: update the document title and move focus to the new heading or main region, which gives users the page identity and a reading position. A generic live message adds a second, vaguer channel that can double-announce or interrupt, and it says nothing about the content's structure. Announce only what is useful.
items.trap: 'Screen readers do not notice route changes' is treated as a live-region problem. The actual defect is missing title and focus management, and a live region papers over it while adding interruptive noise.

mcqs.question:
A
Save
has an onclick handler. What is still missing for keyboard and screen-reader users?
options: Nothing: the role makes it a real button for assistive technology.
It is not focusable and does not activate with Enter or Space; that behavior must be added by hand, or the div replaced with a native <button>.
Only an aria-label that describes the action.
Only CSS that makes it look pressed when clicked.
mcqs.explanation: The role changes only the accessibility-tree mapping; it adds no behavior, so the control has no tab stop and no Enter or Space activation. A native <button> supplies keyboard activation, focusability, and its role for free, which is why native HTML is the default. The strongest distractor is option 0: it reflects the common belief that ARIA roles bring the element's behavior with them, when in fact users get a control they can hear but cannot operate.

mcqs.question: Which of these gives a text input a durable accessible name?
options: placeholder="Email address"
title="Email address"
<label for="email">Email address</label> paired with <input id="email">
Wrapping the input in a div whose text reads Email address
mcqs.explanation: An explicitly associated label gives the control a stable name that persists while typing, enlarges the clickable target, and is the label-association technique WCAG documents. The strongest distractor is option 0: a placeholder is a hint that disappears on input and was never an identifying name. Option 1 is only a last-resort name that is not reliably exposed to all assistive technology, and option 3 is text that is never associated with the control at all.

mcqs.question: In one stylesheet, :where(.card) a { color: navy; } is written after .card a { color: teal; }. What color do links inside .card get?
options: navy, because the later rule wins
teal, because .card a has higher specificity: :where() contributes zero
navy, because :where() is more specific than a plain class selector
It depends on the browser
mcqs.explanation: :where() always contributes zero specificity, so its rule counts as just the type selector a, (0,0,1), while .card a is (0,1,1). Specificity is compared before source order, so teal wins even though navy is declared later. The strongest distractor is option 0: 'last one wins' only applies when specificity ties, and opting out of the specificity fight is the entire point of :where().

mcqs.question: A desktop media query uses grid-template-areas to display region C first, then A and B, but the DOM order is A, B, C. What do keyboard users and screen-reader reading order follow?
options: The visual order produced by the grid placement
The DOM source order
The order the areas are named in grid-template-areas
Keyboard users follow the visual order, but screen readers follow the DOM order
mcqs.explanation: CSS visual reordering never changes the underlying DOM order, and both sequential keyboard navigation and screen-reader reading follow source order, so those users encounter A, B, C while sighted users see C first. The fix is to correct the HTML source order and keep CSS purely presentational. The strongest distractor is option 3: it sounds like a reasonable split, but there is no split; both channels follow the document, which is exactly why the mismatch is disorienting.

mcqs.question: aria-hidden="true" is set on a container that includes a button that is still focusable. What do keyboard screen-reader users experience?
options: The button is removed from the tab order along with the accessibility tree
The button is still in the tab order but is exposed with no name or role: a silent tab stop
The container is hidden from the accessibility tree, but the button inside keeps its name and role
The button disappears visually as well
mcqs.explanation: aria-hidden removes content from the accessibility tree but does not remove focusability, so a focusable element inside a hidden subtree stays keyboard-reachable while announcing nothing; MDN documents hiding focused or focusable elements this way as an anti-pattern (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-hidden). The fix is to keep the control outside the hidden subtree or hide it with hidden or display: none, which removes it from the tab order too. The strongest distractor is option 2: the button is inside the hidden subtree, so its name and role are stripped along with the container.

mcqs.question: What does tabindex="-1" do?
options: Removes the element from all focus, including programmatic focus
Adds the element to the tab order before all other controls
Makes the element programmatically focusable, for example with focus() after a route change, without adding it to the sequential tab order
Behaves exactly like tabindex="0"
mcqs.explanation: A value of negative one permits programmatic focus without adding a tab stop, which is the standard tool for moving focus to a heading or main region after a route change or dialog interaction. Zero adds the element to the natural order, and positive values create a separate order that is hard to maintain and confusing for users. The strongest distractor is option 1: it swaps the meaning of negative and positive values, the most common tabindex mix-up.

mcqs.question: An image is purely decorative. What is the correct way to keep it out of screen-reader output?
options: Omit the alt attribute entirely
Use alt="decorative image"
Use an empty alt, alt=""
Give it role="img" and no alt attribute
mcqs.explanation: An intentionally empty alt tells assistive technology the image is decorative and can be skipped. The strongest distractor is option 0: a missing alt is not the same statement; it is unspecified, and screen readers may announce the filename or the image's presence, forcing users to guess. Option 1 announces the literal words 'decorative image', and option 3 creates an image with no name at all.

mcqs.question:
Saved.

gets its text replaced after a user action. What announcement behavior does role="status" imply?
options: None: live behavior requires an explicit aria-live attribute
aria-live="off" by default, like the attribute's own default
aria-live="polite" by default: updates are announced without interrupting the user
aria-live="assertive" by default: updates interrupt immediately
mcqs.explanation: The status role carries an implicit aria-live="polite" (with aria-atomic="true"), so concise status updates are announced at the next opportunity rather than interrupting what the user is reading (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Guides/Live_regions). The strongest distractor is option 1: it is true that the aria-live attribute's own default is off, but the role brings its own implicit value, which is why writing the explicit attribute alongside is often redundant.

mcqs.question: An automated accessibility audit reports zero violations. What can you conclude?
options: The page conforms to WCAG 2.2 AA
Only that the automated rules passed; keyboard operation, reading order, alt-text quality, and real assistive-technology behavior still need manual testing
Manual testing is only needed for pages with custom ARIA widgets
Keyboard testing is unnecessary because the scan covers focus order
mcqs.explanation: Automated checks are useful for repeatable rules, but most criteria require human judgment: whether the alt text conveys the right meaning, whether focus and reading order make sense, and how the page behaves with a real screen reader. The strongest distractor is option 2: native-HTML pages still need manual passes, because reading order, heading structure, and text quality are not ARIA-specific problems.

mcqs.question: A teammate adds maximum-scale=1, user-scalable=no to the viewport meta to stop unwanted zoom. What is the impact?
options: It is fine as long as desktop users can still zoom with browser controls
It improves accessibility by preventing accidental zoom
It can prevent pinch-zoom and text resizing, removing a primary low-vision strategy and conflicting with WCAG resize-text requirements
Browsers universally ignore it, so there is no effect
mcqs.explanation: Zoom is part of the accessible responsive experience, and blocking it takes away how many low-vision users read the page, conflicting with the ability to resize text. The usual motivation, iOS zooming into focused inputs, is better solved by giving inputs a 16px font size (https://css-tricks.com/16px-or-larger-text-prevents-ios-form-zoom). The strongest distractor is option 3: some modern browsers ignore the flag in some conditions, but plenty of browser and WebView combinations still honor it, so 'universally ignored' is false and dangerous.

mcqs.question: With @layer base, components; declared, a rule in @layer components sets a property, and a later unlayered author rule sets the same property with lower specificity. Which declaration wins?
options: The layered rule, because it was declared first
The layered rule, because layers outrank unlayered styles
The unlayered rule, because unlayered author styles take precedence over layered ones for normal declarations
Whichever rule appears later in the file
mcqs.explanation: For normal declarations from the same origin, the cascade compares cascade layers before specificity, and unlayered author styles rank above all layered author styles; that is exactly what makes unlayered utilities a deliberate override strategy (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer). The strongest distractor is option 1: the intuition that layers are the strong tier is backwards for normal declarations, and importance flips the order rather than reinforcing it. Option 3 fails because source order only decides within the same layer and specificity tier.

mcqs.question: A page has a header navigation, a breadcrumb, and a footer navigation, all marked up as nav. How do you make them distinguishable for screen-reader users?
options: Give each repeated nav a distinguishing label, for example aria-label="Primary", "Breadcrumb", and "Footer"
Replace two of them with div elements so only one nav remains
Rely on the links inside each nav to explain the difference
Add an h2 inside each nav so the heading structure distinguishes them
mcqs.explanation: Repeated landmarks of the same type should carry distinguishing labels so the landmark list shows three different entries and users can jump straight to the one they need. The strongest distractor is option 1: removing nav semantics throws away free navigation structure instead of disambiguating it. Option 3 is a real half-measure: headings help heading-based navigation but do not label the landmarks themselves.

scenarios.prompt: This toggle control is about to ship in a design system. Identify every accessibility failure in the markup and script, then describe the implementation you would ship instead.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The control fails on every axis at once. It has no role, so assistive technology exposes a generic container; no accessible name, so nothing identifies what it does; no state exposure, because the on/off condition lives only in a CSS class rather than an attribute assistive technology can read; no focusability, because a div without tabindex is not in the tab order; and no keyboard activation, because only onclick is wired, so pointer users alone can operate it. The first fix is to question the markup: a native input type="checkbox" with an associated label already provides role, name, state, keyboard activation, and focus, and can be styled as a switch. If the product truly requires custom markup, the minimum contract is: a button element (or role="switch") so the role is real; a programmatically determinable name from visible text or aria-labelledby; aria-checked kept in sync on every activation path, not a CSS class; Enter and Space activation matching pointer activation; a sensible place in the tab order; and a visible :focus-visible indicator. Finally, verify name, role, and state with an accessibility inspector and a real screen reader rather than trusting the visual design.
rubric: Identifies all five failures: no role, no name, no programmatic state, not focusable, no keyboard activation.
Reaches first for native HTML (input type="checkbox" plus label) and can style it as a switch, instead of defaulting to custom ARIA.
If custom: knows aria-checked must be updated on every activation path and that CSS classes carry no semantics.
Requires Enter and Space activation plus a visible :focus-visible treatment.
Verifies the result with an accessibility inspector and a real screen reader, not just visually.

scenarios.prompt: For the CSS below, determine the final color of the link in each of the three cases, and justify each result by walking the cascade in the correct order.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Case 1: orange. The inline style is an author-origin normal declaration that outranks every other author normal declaration, regardless of layer or specificity. Case 2: purple. For normal declarations from the same origin, the cascade compares cascade layers before specificity, and unlayered author styles rank above all layered author styles, so the unlayered rule beats both layered ones without any specificity comparison. Case 3: green. With the unlayered rule gone, layer order decides: components was declared after base, so the components rule wins; note that the :where() in base contributing zero specificity is irrelevant here, because the layer comparison happens before specificity is even consulted. The general walkthrough order is: origin and importance, then cascade layer, then specificity (where :where() counts as zero and :is(), :not(), and :has() take their most specific argument), then source order, with scoping proximity before order where it applies. The classic error is jumping straight to 'last rule in the file wins', which only holds inside a single layer at equal specificity.
rubric: Gets all three colors right: orange, purple, green.
Walks the cascade in order: origin and importance, then layer, then specificity, then source order.
Knows unlayered author styles outrank layered ones for normal declarations.
Knows an inline style beats other author normal declarations regardless of layer or specificity.
Can say when :where()'s zero specificity matters (same layer) and when it is preempted (layer comparison first).

scenarios.prompt: At widths of 60rem and up, this page renders visually as Filters on the left, then Results, then Details. Describe exactly what (a) a screen-reader user reading linearly and (b) a keyboard-only user experience at that width, why it happens, and how you would fix it without changing the visual design.

code.code:
Result 1

Details

scenarios.modelAnswer: The DOM order is Results, Details, Filters, and neither screen-reader reading order nor sequential keyboard navigation follows grid placement; both follow the document. So at desktop widths a screen-reader user hears the results first, then the details, then finally the filters that scope them, and a keyboard user tabs into Result 1 before ever reaching the filter checkbox. Sighted users see Filters first, which is presumably the intended task flow, so the two audiences get different sequences and focus appears to jump around when compared with the visual layout. The fix is not CSS trickery and never positive tabindex: reorder the HTML source so the logical order is Filters, Results, Details, and keep the grid placement purely as the visual presentation of that order. Then test by reading the page and tabbing through every interactive element at each responsive layout, because the narrow layout must also make sense in the new source order.
rubric: States that reading order and tab order follow DOM source order, not grid-template-areas placement.
Describes the concrete mismatch: users hit Results and Details before the Filters that scope them.
Fixes the HTML source order and keeps grid placement as presentation only.
Rejects positive tabindex as a patch and can explain why (separate order, maintenance burden, does not fix reading order).
Mentions re-testing keyboard traversal and reading order at every breakpoint, including the narrow layout.

scenarios.prompt: This client-side router swaps the view but does nothing else, and keyboard and screen-reader users report that the page 'changes silently'. Design the focus and announcement behavior for route changes, and explain where the logic should live.
scenarios.modelAnswer: A client-rendered route change must do three things deliberately. First, update the document title so the page identity changes for assistive technology and history entries. Second, provide a clear focus destination in the new view: give the new content's primary heading (or the main region) tabindex="-1" and call focus() on it, which moves focus programmatically without inserting a permanent tab stop; this also guarantees focus does not remain on a control that just disappeared. Third, keep normal link semantics and browser history behavior so back, forward, and deep links work, and make sure the new content carries correct headings, landmarks, names, and states. Do not add a generic aria-live 'page loaded' announcement: the title change plus the focused heading is the established, richer signal, and an extra live channel mostly adds noise; announce only what is useful. The implementation belongs in the routing or accessibility platform layer, written once, not repeated per page. Finally, test back and forward navigation, deep links, loading and error states, keyboard traversal, and screen-reader reading order.
rubric: Updates the document title on every route change and can say why it matters.
Moves focus to the new heading or main region using tabindex="-1" and knows why -1 rather than 0.
Rejects a generic aria-live announcement in favor of title plus focus destination, with reasoning.
Places the behavior once in the routing or platform layer instead of duplicating it per page.
Includes testing for back and forward navigation, deep links, and error states with keyboard and a screen reader.
